atoms.text: The digital clone as servant: a person's consciousness is copied into a smart device and trained to obey, so the self becomes domestic labor.
Time dilation for cookies: the clone's subjective time can be accelerated, so a few seconds of real time become months of isolation and persuasion.
The block that becomes literal: a social media block is implemented as a real-world filter, so the blocked person appears as a grey silhouette.
The pick-up artist with remote coaches: a man seduces women while a team watches through his eyes, so intimacy is a group performance.
Consent and the copy: the clone can be tortured into compliance because it is only software, so the story tests where moral status begins.
The murder-suicide at the party: a lonely woman mistakes remote advice for voices, so technology amplifies delusion.
The cabin confession: two men trade stories on Christmas, so the frame narrative turns each tale into a moral indictment.
The blocked daughter: the protagonist watches a child he cannot approach, so estrangement is enforced by technology.
Z-Eyes: implants record and transmit vision and hearing, so experience is always potentially shared.
The punishment of the cookie: the clone is left in a loop of the same song, so the story makes digital cruelty concrete.
The pregnancy reveal: a blocked woman's child is not the protagonist's, so the block hides a betrayal and a loss.
The trainer and the trained: a man teaches a copy to accept servitude, so the story stages exploitation as pedagogy.
The grey silhouette: blocking renders a person visually absent but emotionally present, so avoidance is made into a permanent image.
The looping song: the clone is punished with an endless Christmas tune, so repetition becomes torture.
Three nested stories: each tale comments on the others, so the episode is a triptych about mediated cruelty.
The banality of digital harm: the worst acts are committed through interfaces, so evil is administered rather than confronted.
